title: TLS Handshake: How Secure Connections Start

scenes.line1: Why does HTTPS take extra time?
scenes.say: Ever wonder why secure sites take a little longer to load? Let's break down what really happens in a TLS handshake.

rows.b: Both sides agree on encryption keys

scenes.say: First, your browser says hello with its supported versions and ciphers, plus the site name. The server replies with its choices and a certificate. Then, both sides agree on keys. After that, everything is encrypted.

scenes.label: Speed
scenes.sub: TLS version one point three does all this in one round trip.
scenes.say: With TLS version one point three, the whole handshake finishes in just one round trip, making secure connections much faster.

scenes.title: See the handshake in action
scenes.say: You can watch this handshake happen using the openssl client tool. It shows every step, including the certificate chain.

scenes.question: Why test TLS by IP can fail?
scenes.wrong: The server always sends the right certificate.
scenes.right: Without the server name, you get the default certificate, which may not match your site.
scenes.say: Here's a common interview trap: If you test TLS by connecting to an IP address without sending the server name, you'll likely get the default certificate, not the one for your site.
